newsitem.title: USA: U.S. states fiscally sound but nervous - governors.
newsitem.headline: U.S. states fiscally sound but nervous - governors.

text.p: The 50 U.S. states are generally in very sound fiscal shape, but they are "casting a cautious eye" toward the future, the National Governors Association reported on Tuesday.

"Governors are keeping a tight grip on spending and are preparing for the uncertainties in the future," Raymond Scheppach, association executive director, told a press briefing in which he released the NGA's annual "Fiscal Survey of States."
"Today, governors are committed to reducing taxes and making state programs more efficient," Scheppach said.
He said state spending in fiscal 1996 rose only 4.5 percent, and the rise is likely to be just 4.0 percent in fiscal 1997.
That compares with an average annual rise of 6.8 percent over the last 20 years, and an average annual rise of about 8.0 percent in the decade 1980-90, he said.
"Spending is really running only about half" of what it was in the past 20 years, Sheppach said.
Sheppach said states are reining in spending because of uncertainty about upcoming modifications in federal spending.
"We don't know what the financial implications of welfare reform are going to be over the next several years," he said.

He also said that after five years of expansion there are questions about whether the economy will turn down in the next year or so. He added, "The federal government is getting a lot more serious about reducing the deficit and, therefore, some states' programs are in jeopardy."
Finally, states are nervous because the federal government is also considering some fairly major tax cuts, Sheppach said.

Sheppach said general fund spending in seven states had grown less than three percent in fiscal 1996 and was projected to remain low in fiscal 1997. The states are Alaska, Hawaii, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Vermont.
He said all regions of the country are likely to experience steady economic growth through fiscal 1997, with the Rocky Mountain, Southeast and Southwest regions once again leading the way.
The New England and Mid-Atlantic regions are the most sluggish, while California's economy has rebounded, he said.
Asked for predictions on infrastructure spending, Sheppach said he sees a "conservative wind blowing."
"I don't see any real boost in school construction and highways," he said.
